query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: Under simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, the accelerated degradation in a multi‐phase eutectic high‐entropy alloy is driven by the mechanical removal of nascent, protective oxide layers at the phase boundaries, which exposes chemically active interfaces that preferentially corrode, thereby creating a synergistic effect that accelerates the overall degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure comprising alternating soft fcc and hard intermetallic (e.g., B2) phases.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous sliding wear (mechanical stress) and a corrosive (oxidizing) environment at elevated temperature (e.g., up to 700°C) that encourages dynamic oxide formation and removal.
generation.conditions: High temperature conditions in an oxidizing atmosphere where both wear forces and corrosion processes are active; tests compared under combined wear-corrosion versus isolated wear-only or corrosion-only scenarios.
generation.structural_mediator: Phase boundaries within the lamellar structure where differences in chemistry and mechanical properties lead to differential oxidation and mechanical stability.
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, a thin protective oxide forms on both phases; however, mechanical wear selectively removes the oxide at the phase boundaries. This leads to exposure of fresh, chemically active surfaces that undergo preferential corrosion due to galvanic differences between phases. The repeated cycle of oxide removal and corrosive attack at these interfaces results in a synergistic acceleration of both wear and corrosion degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to a matched baseline (exposure to either wear or corrosion alone), the total degradation (combined material loss) will increase significantly. Individually, the wear rate is expected to be higher due to the lack of a robust protective oxide, and the corrosion rate will be elevated at the phase boundaries, giving rise to localized deep penetration corrosion that would not be as prominent under isolated conditions.
generation.baseline: A matched specimen of the same eutectic HEA under conditions of either wear-only in an inert environment or corrosion-only without mechanical wear at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold under conditions where temperature and oxidizing environment allow for the formation of moderate protective oxide layers, and where wear forces are sufficient to disrupt these layers but not so extreme as to cause wholesale mechanical failure independent of corrosion.
generation.uncertainty: The relative contributions of mechanical wear versus chemical corrosion to the overall degradation remain to be quantitatively established, and variations in phase boundary chemistry or microstructural scale may alter the coupling intensity of the degradation processes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of identical eutectic HEA samples with the same lamellar microstructure. Pre-oxidize one set by a controlled thermal treatment to develop a thicker, more stable oxide layer on all surfaces (especially at phase boundaries). Subject both sets to identical simultaneous wear-corrosion testing at elevated temperature. The control would be the as-cast (non-preoxidized) samples, and an additional baseline could be groups exposed to wear-only or corrosion-only.
measurements: Quantitative wear loss (via mass loss measurements and profilometry)
Corrosion rate (using electrochemical impedance spectroscopy or equivalent techniques)
Microstructural examination (via SEM/TEM imaging) to assess oxide layer continuity and phase interface integrity
Oxide layer thickness measurements (possibly using XPS or TEM)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-oxidized samples (with a thicker and more stable oxide at phase boundaries) do not show a significant reduction in total degradation (both wear and localized corrosion) compared to the non-preoxidized samples under identical testing conditions, then the hypothesis—that accelerated degradation is driven by the mechanical disruption of protective oxide layers at phase boundaries—would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
A Promising New Class of High-Temperature Alloys: Eutectic High-Entropy Alloys

Abstract: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Evidence of Inverse Hall-Petch Behavior and Low Friction and Wear in High Entropy Alloys

Abstract: AbstractWe present evidence of inverse Hall-Petch behavior for a single-phase high entropy alloy (CoCrFeMnNi) in ultra-high vacuum and show that it is associated with low friction coefficients (~0.3). Grain size measurements by STEM validate a recently proposed dynamic amorphization model that accurately predicts grain size-dependent shear strength in the inverse Hall-Petch regime. Wear rates in the initially soft (coarse grained) material were shown to be remarkably low (~10–6 mm3/N-m), the lowest for any HEA tested in an inert environment where oxidation and the formation of mixed metal-oxide films is mitigated. The combined high wear resistance and low friction are linked to the formation of an ultra-nanocrystalline near-surface layer. The dynamic amorphization model was also used to predict an average high angle grain boundary energy (0.87 J/m2). This value was used to explain cavitation-induced nanoporosity found in the highly deformed surface layer, a phenomenon that has been linked to superplasticity.Subject terms: Structural materials, Structural properties
